Psuche
psoo-KHAY
noun
Greek psychē (ψυχη), “soul, life, breath”; rendered soul, life, and mind in the Authorized Version.

Biblical Definition

Psuche is the Greek word of the New Testament for the soul, the life, the inner self of man, and it carries the whole weight of what is at stake in salvation. The Lord Jesus uses it in the most solemn warnings: what is a man profited if he shall gain the whole world and lose his own psuche—his own soul—and what shall a man give in exchange for it? Fear not them which kill the body but are not able to kill the soul; rather fear Him who is able to destroy both soul and body in hell. The same word names the life that is laid down and taken up: he that will save his psuche shall lose it, and he that loseth it for Christ’s sake shall find it. It is the soul that magnifies the Lord in Mary’s song, the soul that prospers in John’s blessing, the soul that is the anchor-hold of the believer’s hope. Scripture knows man as body and soul—not a body merely, nor a soul imprisoned in flesh, but an embodied soul created by God, the soul outlasting the death of the body and accountable to its Maker. The dictionary reads psuche as the immortal inner self whose eternal welfare is the chief concern of the gospel: the soul gained or lost forever, worth more than the whole world, redeemed by the blood of Christ.

Key Scripture

Mat 16:26 — "For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?"

Mat 10:28 — "And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell."

Luk 1:46 — "And Mary said, My soul doth magnify the Lord,"

3Jo 1:2 — "Beloved, I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth."

Modern Corruption

Materialism denies the soul outright, and annihilationism denies its immortality; Scripture knows man as an embodied soul, the soul outlasting the body and accountable to God.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two errors press against the biblical psuche. The first is materialism, which denies the soul altogether, reducing man to brain and chemistry, so that there is nothing in him to gain or lose, judge or save. The second is annihilationism, which grants a soul but denies its immortality, teaching that the wicked are snuffed out rather than punished forever—against the Lord’s own warning of Him who is able to destroy both soul and body in hell, and against the everlasting weight His words give to the soul’s gain or loss. If the soul could be gained and lost for an hour only, the bargain of the whole world would not be so terrible.

The principle to recover is the immortal, accountable soul. Man is an embodied soul made by God; the psuche outlasts the death of the body and stands before its Maker. This is why the Lord prizes one soul above the whole world and why the gospel labors for the soul’s eternal welfare. To deny the soul is to empty salvation of its object; to deny its immortality is to dull the urgency of the cross. The believer’s soul magnifies the Lord now and is kept by Him for ever.
